title: Isolation Levels
subtitle: Understanding concurrency anomalies (Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantom Reads, Write Skew) and ANSI SQL guarantees.
keyTakeaways: Isolation levels represent an architectural compromise between transaction concurrency and the tolerance of data read anomalies.
Most production databases do NOT default to true Serializable isolation; PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed, while MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read (Snapshot Isolation).
Snapshot Isolation prevents non-repeatable reads and phantoms, but remains vulnerable to Write Skew unless guarded by explicit row locks or serializable concurrency.
architectureDiagram:
ISOLATION LEVELS & ANOMALY SPECTRUM
Isolation Level       | Dirty Reads | Non-Repeatable Reads | Phantoms | Write Skew
---------------------+-------------+----------------------+----------+------------
Read Uncommitted     | YES (Allowed)| YES                  | YES      | YES
Read Committed (PG)  | NO          | YES (Allowed)        | YES      | YES
Repeatable Read (MY) | NO          | NO                   | NO (MVCC)| YES (Vulnerable!)
Serializable         | NO          | NO                   | NO       | NO (Strict)

sections.heading: Concurrency Anomalies Explained
sections.body: When transactions execute concurrently, performance demands running them simultaneously rather than one by one. The ANSI SQL standard defines four isolation levels based on which anomalies they prevent.
bullets: Dirty Read: Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B commits. If Transaction B rolls back, Transaction A acted on phantom data that never officially existed.
Non-Repeatable Read (Fuzzy Read): Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates that row and commits, and Transaction A re-reads the row to find different values.

Phantom Read: Transaction A queries a range of rows (`WHERE salary > 100k`), Transaction B inserts a new row matching that condition and commits, and Transaction A re-executes the query to find newly appeared rows.

Write Skew: Two transactions read overlapping data, find that business constraints are satisfied, and perform disjoint writes that collectively violate the constraint (e.g., two on-call doctors simultaneously unregistering because both saw two active doctors).

sections.heading: How Engines Implement Isolation Levels in Practice
sections.body: Understanding the difference between theory and implementation is critical. While ANSI SQL was written assuming lock-based concurrency (Two-Phase Locking), modern relational engines implement isolation via MVCC snapshots.
bullets: Read Committed (Postgres Default): Each individual query within a transaction takes a fresh MVCC snapshot. Eliminates dirty reads, but allows non-repeatable reads if another transaction commits between queries.
Repeatable Read (MySQL Default): The transaction takes a single MVCC snapshot at the moment of the first read. All subsequent reads see that identical snapshot, eliminating non-repeatable reads.

Serializable (SSI): PostgreSQL implements Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects overlapping read/write dependencies in memory without locking rows, aborting one of the conflicting transactions with a serialization failure (`40001`).

tradeOffs.pros: Maximum transaction throughput; minimal lock contention; zero serialization rollback failures.
tradeOffs.cons: Queries within the same transaction can observe changing row values; vulnerable to lost updates.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Standard CRUD applications, read-heavy dashboard APIs, and general web applications.

tradeOffs.pros: Mathematically guarantees zero concurrency anomalies, phantoms, or write skew; simplified application reasoning.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher abort rates under write contention; requires application-layer retry loops on serialization failures.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Complex financial auditing, multi-account ledger balancing, and legal contract state machines.

interviewTip: Highlight Write Skew to demonstrate senior-level database knowledge: 'Snapshot Isolation (Repeatable Read) does not prevent Write Skew. If two concurrent transactions read overlapping state and update different rows to violate a shared business rule, both will commit. Preventing Write Skew requires either true Serializable isolation or explicit pessimistic row locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.'
